“Certainly, sir. It also has the advantage of being popular in less refined societies. Every savage knows how to dance.”

Sir William merely smiled. After a pause, seeing Bingley join them, he continued, “Your friend dances wonderfully. I'm sure you are very skilled at it yourself, Mr. Darcy.”

“You saw me dance at Meryton, I believe, sir.”

“Indeed I did, and I greatly enjoyed the sight. Do you often dance at St. James's?”

“Never, sir.”

“Don't you think it would show proper respect for the place?”

“It's a form of respect I avoid paying anywhere if I can.”

“I assume you have a house in London?”

Mr. Darcy bowed.

“I once considered settling there myself, since I enjoy the best society. But I wasn't certain London's air would suit Lady Lucas.”

He paused, hoping for a reply, but his companion had no wish to offer one. Just then Elizabeth came towards them. Sir William thought of what seemed to him a wonderfully gallant gesture and called to her:

“My dear Miss Eliza, why aren't you dancing? Mr. Darcy, let me introduce this young lady as an excellent partner. I'm sure you can't refuse to dance with such beauty before you.” He took her hand and was about to place it in Mr. Darcy's. Though very surprised, Darcy was willing to accept it. But she immediately drew back and spoke to Sir William with some agitation.

“Really, sir, I have no intention of dancing. Please don't imagine that I walked this way to beg for a partner.”

Mr. Darcy politely and seriously asked her to honor him with a dance, but without success. Elizabeth would not change her mind, and Sir William's attempts to persuade her made no difference.

“You dance so well, Miss Eliza, that it's cruel to deny me the pleasure of watching you. And although this gentleman generally dislikes dancing, I'm certain he wouldn't object to pleasing us for half an hour.”

“Mr. Darcy is all politeness,” Elizabeth said with a smile.

“He certainly is. But considering the attraction, my dear Miss Eliza, we can hardly be surprised by his willingness. Who could object to such a partner?”

Elizabeth gave a mischievous look and turned away. Her refusal had not lowered her in the gentleman's opinion. He was thinking of her with some satisfaction when Miss Bingley addressed him:

They both expressed their distress at the dreadful outcome Elizabeth thought almost certain, and which Miss Bennet could not say was impossible. Then Elizabeth continued, “But tell me everything I haven't heard yet. Give me all the details. What did Colonel Forster say? Had they suspected nothing before the elopement? They must have seen them together constantly.”

“Colonel Forster admitted he'd often noticed signs of affection, especially from Lydia, but nothing that alarmed him. I feel so sorry for him. He has been as kind and attentive as anyone could be. He was already planning to visit us to express his concern before he had any reason to think they hadn't gone to Scotland. When that fear first arose, he hurried his journey.”

“And was Denny certain Wickham wouldn't marry her? Did he know they planned to run away? Had Colonel Forster spoken to Denny himself?”

“Yes. But when the Colonel questioned him, Denny denied knowing anything about their plans and wouldn't give his true opinion. He didn't repeat his belief that they wouldn't marry. That makes me hope someone misunderstood him before.”

“So until Colonel Forster arrived, none of you doubted that they were really married?”

“How could such an idea have occurred to us? I felt a little uneasy, a little afraid for my sister's happiness as his wife, because I knew his behavior hadn't always been right. Our father and mother knew nothing about that. They only thought how unwise the marriage must be. Kitty then admitted, naturally rather pleased to know more than the rest of us, that Lydia's last letter had prepared her for something like this. Apparently she'd known for weeks that they were in love.”

“But not before they went to Brighton?”

“No, I don't believe so.”

“And did Colonel Forster himself seem to think badly of Wickham? Does he know what he's really like?”

“I have to admit that he didn't speak as well of Wickham as he used to. He thought him careless and extravagant. Since this sad affair happened, people have said he left Meryton owing a great deal of money. But I hope that isn't true.”

“Oh, Jane! If we'd kept less to ourselves and told people what we knew about him, this couldn't have happened!”

“Perhaps that would have been better,” her sister replied.

“But it seemed wrong to reveal someone's past faults without knowing how they felt or whether they had changed.”

He wrote that he was wasting his time where he was. The friends he had made in London had sent letters asking him to return and finish the negotiations for his venture in India. He could no longer postpone leaving. But his journey to London might lead to his longer voyage even sooner than he expected, and he begged me to spend as much time with him as I could. He therefore asked me to leave my lonely island and meet him at Perth, so we could travel south together. His letter brought me back to life a little, and I decided to leave the island in two days.

Before going, however, I had a task to do that made me shudder. I had to pack my chemical instruments. That meant entering the room where I had carried out my hateful work and touching the tools whose very appearance made me feel sick. At daybreak the next morning, I gathered enough courage to unlock the laboratory. Pieces of the unfinished creature I had destroyed lay scattered across the floor. I almost felt as though I had torn apart the living flesh of a human being. I stopped to steady myself, then entered. My hands shook as I carried the instruments out. But I realized I must not leave the remains of my work behind to frighten the local people and arouse their suspicions. I put the remains in a basket with a large number of stones, set it aside, and resolved to throw it into the sea that night. Meanwhile, I sat on the beach cleaning and arranging my chemical equipment.

My feelings had changed completely since the night the demon appeared. Before then, I had regarded my promise with dark despair as something I must carry out, whatever the consequences. Now I felt as if a covering had been lifted from my eyes and I could see clearly for the first time. The thought of returning to my work never entered my mind, even for an instant. His threat weighed heavily on me, but I did not think of preventing it by an action of my own. I had firmly decided that creating another being like the fiend I had already made would be an act of the most vile and terrible selfishness. I drove away every thought that might lead me to any other conclusion.
